q: When is the safest time for urgent non-obstetric surgery during pregnancy?
why: The first trimester carries teratogenic and miscarriage risk; the third carries preterm labour risk.

q: Why should NSAIDs be avoided after surgery in pregnancy?
o: Risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
why: NSAIDs can close the fetal ductus arteriosus prematurely.

q: What intra-abdominal pressure is recommended for laparoscopy in pregnancy?
why: Keep pressure under about 12 mmHg, control EtCO2 and use an open entry technique.

q: Why might neostigmine with glycopyrronium cause fetal bradycardia?
o: Neostigmine crosses but glycopyrronium does not
why: Some neostigmine crosses while glycopyrronium does not, so atropine is sometimes preferred.

q: Which drug barely crosses the placenta because of its large molecular size?
why: Drugs over about 1,000 Da (heparin, insulin) barely cross; muscle relaxants cross minimally.

q: What is ion trapping of local anaesthetics in the fetus?
o: Weak bases become more ionised in the more acidic fetus and are trapped
Drugs are metabolised by the placenta
why: Fetal pH is lower; a fetal acidosis worsens trapping.

q: Which tocolytic is a competitive oxytocin receptor antagonist?
why: Atosiban; beta-2 agonists, nifedipine, GTN and volatiles also relax the uterus.

q: In multiple sclerosis, what happens to relapse rates in pregnancy?
o: They rise in the third trimester
They fall in pregnancy and rise postpartum
why: Relapses fall during pregnancy and rise after delivery; a standard spinal is now considered reasonable.

q: Which analgesic should breastfeeding mothers avoid?
why: Avoid codeine, tramadol and aspirin; most anaesthetic drugs transfer minimally.

q: How should fetal wellbeing be managed around non-obstetric surgery after viability?
o: Fetal heart monitoring before and after (or continuous CTG where appropriate), with obstetric input
why: Liaise with obstetrics about fetal monitoring, tocolysis and steroids.
